title: The Breakfast Express

topics.value_lesson: Kids everywhere eat breakfast, but it looks different in different places—and there's no one right way to eat

spine: A magical breakfast train carries a child around the world to discover how kids everywhere start their day with different foods and different ways of eating.

segments.text: Morning. Just barely. {hero_name} stands on the platform, and the whole sky is the color of warm toast. Right in front of us, a long green train hums softly — and look. Look at the steam. It curls up from the roof, thick as soup, as porridge, as the warm breath of someone still sleeping. A whistle goes. Toot-toot! Then — clang! — a woman in a bright red cap swings down from the front car. "You're here! You're here!" she says. "I'm Conductor Zara, and this is the Breakfast Express. We ride all around the world, tasting how kids start their day." She holds out her hand. "Somewhere right now, a kid is eating warm rice for breakfast. Somewhere else, it's flatbread with honey. Want to come see?" We look at the steam. We look at her big smile. We climb aboard.

The train slows. Whoo-ooosh. "Japan!" calls Zara. We step off into a small warm kitchen. Steam curls up from a bowl of rice, thick as soup, as porridge, as breath on a cold morning. A grandmother smiles. "For breakfast," she says, "we crack an egg on top. Like this." Tap. Crack. Plop. The yolk sits on the rice, golden as a tiny sun. She stirs with chopsticks, and the sun melts into the grains. "Now you," she says, and hands us a pair. {hero_name} pinches them tight. The rice slips. It slides. It will not stay. "Slow," she says gently. "Like picking up a little bird." We breathe out. We try again.

The train slows. Whoo-ooosh. "Ethiopia!" calls Zara. We step off into a kitchen that smells like warm bread and spice. On the table lies a big round injera, soft and spongy, with steam still curling off it. A father tears a piece with one hand. "Like this," he says. "Then scoop." He folds it around a spoonful of red lentils and pops it in his mouth. "Now you." {hero_name} grabs the edge and pulls. Rrrrip! The piece is huge, bigger than our whole hand. Everyone laughs, kind and warm, and we laugh too. "A little smaller," he says, smiling. "Try again."

Back on the train, the whistle goes. Toot-toot! The Breakfast Express hums and rolls. Conductor Zara leans close. "What did you find out there?" she asks. We tell her, and her eyes go wide and bright. "Steam rising," she says softly. "Warm food. Kids eating breakfast in all kinds of ways." Outside the window, the world slides by — green hills, then rooftops, then streets waking up. The train rocks us gently, side to side, like bathwater. Zara stands up tall. "Next stop," she says, "a busy street corner in Vietnam. Somewhere right now, a kid is slurping noodles for breakfast." Slurping! We look at the steam curling from the roof. We look at her big smile. The whistle sings again, and the train hurries on, deeper into morning.

The train stops. Steam everywhere! It curls from a big pot on the street corner, thick as soup. A cook smiles at us. "Pho for breakfast," she says. With long chopsticks, she lifts slippery noodles from the bubbling pot. Swish! Into a bowl they go. "Somewhere right now, a kid is slurping these," Zara whispers. The cook hands {hero_name} small chopsticks. "Try!" We pinch. We lift. A noodle wiggles... and plop! Back it splashes. Everyone smiles, and we try again. This time — slurp! Warm broth, soft noodles. Our whole belly goes cozy. The cook wraps up chopsticks for {hero_name} to keep. "For home," she says. We climb aboard, holding them tight, tasting that warm soup all the way back.

The train stops. Steam curls from a little bakery door, sweet and warm. Inside, a baker with flour on her nose smiles. "For breakfast," she says, "we dip." She hands {hero_name} a piece of baguette, still warm, and a bowl of hot chocolate. "Somewhere right now, a kid is dipping bread just like this," Zara whispers. We dip. We lift. Drip, drip! Sweet chocolate drops on the table. The baker laughs softly and slides us a napkin. "It means the chocolate is good," she says. We bite. Crunch, then soft, then warm chocolate. Our whole mouth is happy. The baker wraps a small baguette for {hero_name} to carry home. "For later," she says. We climb aboard, holding it close, the taste of dipping still on our lips.
